title: Pyra et fuga. Mercurius
titleEn: The Pyre, Mercury's Warning and the Flight — Aeneid IV.504–606
part: The Pyre, Mercury's Warning and the Flight (IV.504–606)
about: Dido has a pyre raised in the inner court, open to the sky, and hangs it with garlands and funeral boughs. On it she lays the clothes, the sword and the likeness of Aeneas, and the priestess calls on the gods of the dead; herbs, false water from Avernus and a love-charm are brought, and Dido, one foot bare and her robe loosened, calls the gods and the stars to witness and prays. It is night, and all the world is asleep, but not Dido: love and anger rise in her again, and she asks herself what she is to do. Go back to the suitors she has scorned? Follow the Trojans and beg? Who would take her aboard, and what of the perjury of Laomedon's race? She tells herself to die, blames Anna, and mourns the vow she broke to Sychaeus. Meanwhile Aeneas sleeps on his high stern, ready to sail. Mercury comes again in a dream, in his old shape, and tells him to flee at once: Dido is plotting, set on death, and if dawn finds him there the sea will be full of ships and fire. The god ends by saying that woman is always inconstant. Aeneas wakes in terror, rouses his men, prays to the unknown god and cuts the cables with his sword; the fleet is away in a rush. At daybreak Dido sees the empty harbour from her watch-towers, beats her breast and tears her hair, and breaks into a storm of orders and self-reproach: she should have torn Aeneas apart, killed his men and his son, burned the fleet and herself on top of it. The speech runs on past the end of this part.

sentences.t:
At regina, pyra penetrali in sede sub auras
erecta ingenti taedis atque ilice secta,
intenditque locum sertis, et fronde coronat
funerea; super exuvias ensemque relictum
effigiemque toro locat, haud ignara futuri.
sentences.l:
But the queen, a pyre in the inmost seat, up to the skies,
having been raised, huge, with pine-wood and cleft oak,
both hangs the place about with garlands and with foliage crowns it
funeral; above, the garments and the sword left behind
and the likeness on the couch she lays, not ignorant of what is to come.
sentences.i: But the queen, with a vast pyre raised in the heart of the palace, open to the sky, built of pine-wood and split oak, hangs the place with garlands, crowns it with funeral boughs, and lays upon the couch the clothes, the sword he left behind, and his likeness, knowing well what is to come.
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'pyra… erecta… taedis atque ilice secta' is an ablative absolute, 'the pyre having been raised', and 'ingenti' (ablative) agrees with 'pyra'; 'secta' (perfect passive participle, 'cut, split') agrees with 'ilice', the holm-oak. 'penetrali in sede… sub auras' is the inner court of the palace, open to the sky: the pyre Dido asked Anna to build (494–497) in the name of a charm. 'intenditque locum sertis' means 'stretches (hangs) the place with garlands'. 'funerea' is the adjective 'funereal', held to the start of the next line, agreeing with 'fronde'. 'exuvias… ensemque relictum… effigiem': the clothes, the sword and the likeness he left behind; 'toro' is the marriage couch, with 'super' ('above') governing no case here. 'haud ignara futuri' is a litotes, 'knowing well', with 'futuri' a genitive of respect.

sentences.t:
Stant arae circum, et crines effusa sacerdos
ter centum tonat ore deos, Erebumque Chaosque,
tergeminamque Hecaten, tria virginis ora Dianae.
sentences.l:
Altars stand around, and with hair loosed the priestess
thrice a hundred gods thunders out with her mouth, Erebus and Chaos,
and threefold Hecate, the three faces of the maiden Diana.
sentences.i: Altars stand round about. With her hair streaming, the priestess calls in a voice of thunder on three hundred gods, on Erebus and Chaos, on three-fold Hecate and the three faces of the maiden Diana.
sentences.n: 'crines effusa' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library has 'crinis') is a passive participle with an accusative of respect: 'having had her hair loosened', literally 'poured out as to her hair'. You will see this Greek-style accusative with passive participles again at 518 and 589. The priestess is the Massylian whom Dido described (483–498). 'ter centum' is three hundred, a round number for 'all the gods'. 'tonat' means 'thunders', a loud incantation. Erebus and Chaos are the dark powers of the underworld; Hecate (Greek accusative 'Hecaten') is the goddess of witchcraft and crossroads, identified with Diana (Artemis) and with the moon: hence 'tria virginis ora Dianae', Diana's three faces (Luna in the sky, Diana on earth, Hecate below).

sentences.i: She had sprinkled, too, water made to look like the spring of Avernus; and herbs, ripe and downy, reaped by moonlight with bronze sickles, are sought, full of the milk of black poison;
sentences.n: 'Sparserat' is a pluperfect, 'had sprinkled' (the priestess is the subject). 'latices simulatos fontis Averni' is 'waters made to look like the spring of Avernus', the lake that was an entrance to the underworld; the water is a stand-in for the real thing. Greenough's 'aënis' has a diaeresis to show that 'a-ë-nis' is three syllables; the Latin Library prints 'aenis'. 'messae' (from 'meto') means 'reaped'; the cutting by the light of the moon is part of the magic. 'pubentes' means 'downy, grown ripe'. 'quaeruntur' is a passive present, 'are sought'. The 'milk' of a plant is its juice; Latin uses 'cum lacte veneni' for 'with the sap of poison'.

sentences.t:
quaeritur et nascentis equi de fronte revolsus
et matri praereptus amor.
sentences.l:
sought too is, from the brow of a newborn foal torn away
and snatched before the mother, love.
sentences.i: and the love-charm too is sought, torn from the forehead of a newborn foal and snatched away before its mother could have it.
sentences.n: 'amor' is here the love-charm itself, a fleshy growth that, in ancient belief, appeared on the forehead of a newborn foal and was eaten by the mother at once; the Greeks called it 'hippomanes'. It was used in love-potions. 'revolsus' (Greenough's spelling, 'revulsus' elsewhere) agrees with 'amor' and so does 'praereptus', 'snatched in advance'. 'quaeritur' repeats the verb from 513 at the head of the clause. 516 is a half-line (hemistich), one of Virgil's unfinished lines (compare 4.44, 4.361, 4.400 and 4.503 earlier in this book); it has eight syllables, so no hexameter fits.

sentences.t:
Ipsa mola manibusque piis altaria iuxta,
unum exuta pedem vinclis, in veste recincta,
testatur moritura deos et conscia fati
sidera;
sentences.l:
She herself, with the meal and with pious hands, beside the altars,
one foot bare of its fastenings, in her robe ungirded,
calls to witness, about to die, the gods and the stars
conscious of fate;
sentences.i: Herself, with the sacred meal and reverent hands, beside the altars, one foot freed from its bindings, her gown unbelted, she calls on the gods to witness, and on the stars that know her fate, as one about to die;
sentences.n: 'mola' is the sacred meal, coarse meal mixed with salt, scattered on the victim and the altar. 'unum exuta pedem vinclis': 'exuta' is a passive participle with the accusative of respect 'pedem' and an ablative of separation, 'freed as to one foot from its fastenings'; the freed foot and the loosened robe are usually taken as the dress of magic ritual, in which nothing binds the worshipper. 'testatur' is the deponent 'testor', 'calls to witness', with accusatives 'deos' and 'sidera'. 'moritura' is a future participle, 'about to die', and 'conscia fati' is an adjective with a genitive: 'sidera conscia fati' means 'stars that share the knowledge of (her) fate'. The Latin Library has 'amantis' in the next line; see the next unit.

sentences.t:
tum, si quod non aequo foedere amantes
curae numen habet iustumque memorque, precatur.
sentences.l:
then, if any divinity lovers in an unequal pact
holds as a care, both just and mindful, she prays.
sentences.i: and then she prays to any power, just and unforgetting, that may have a care for lovers bound by an unequal pact.
sentences.n: 'tum' continues the list of her acts. 'si quod… numen habet' means 'if any divine power (there is that) holds': 'quod' is the indefinite adjective after 'si'. 'amantes' (Greenough; the Latin Library has 'amantis') is the object of 'habet', and 'curae' is a dative of purpose, 'as a care', so 'habet amantes curae' is 'has lovers as a care'. 'non aequo foedere' is an ablative of manner or description: 'in an uneven pact', bound on unequal terms. 'iustumque memorque' pairs two adjectives with 'numen'; 'memor' means mindful. It is a prayer with no certainty, 'if there is any god'.

sentences.t:
Nox erat, et placidum carpebant fessa soporem
corpora per terras, silvaeque et saeva quierant
aequora:
sentences.l:
It was night, and a calm sleep were taking, weary,
bodies over the lands, and the woods and the savage
seas had grown quiet:
sentences.i: It was night; across the lands tired creatures were taking the gentle quiet of sleep, and the woods and the savage seas had sunk to rest:
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'Nox erat' begins a famous night-piece, which readers compare with the scene in Apollonius of Rhodes where Medea alone lies awake; Dido too lies awake while all else sleeps. 'fessa… corpora' is split by the object 'soporem': 'weary bodies', meaning living creatures. 'carpebant' means 'were plucking, taking, enjoying' (as at 555, said of Aeneas). 'quierant' is a syncopated pluperfect, 'quieverant', 'had fallen quiet'. The colon opens a long time clause: 'cum… cum…'.

sentences.t:
cum medio volvuntur sidera lapsu,
cum tacet omnis ager, pecudes pictaeque volucres,
sentences.l:
when in mid-glide the stars roll on,
when every field is silent, the herds and the painted birds,
sentences.i: in the hour when the stars roll in the middle of their gliding course, when every field lies silent, and the cattle and the bright-feathered birds,
sentences.n: 'cum medio volvuntur sidera lapsu' means 'when the stars roll in their mid-course': the dead of night. 'lapsu' is an ablative of attendant circumstance; 'medio… lapsu' is 'in the midst of the glide'. 'tacet omnis ager, pecudes pictaeque volucres' has 'omnis ager' as the subject of 'tacet'; 'pecudes' ('herds') and 'volucres' ('winged things') are added as a loose list, and are among the subjects of the verb 'lenibant' still to come. 'pictae' means 'painted', i.e. bright-coloured.

sentences.t:
quaeque lacus late liquidos, quaeque aspera dumis
rura tenent, somno positae sub nocte silenti
[lenibant curas, et corda oblita laborum.]
sentences.l:
and those which lakes far and wide liquid, and those which rough with thickets
fields hold, set down in sleep beneath the silent night,
[were soothing their cares, and hearts forgetful of toils.]
sentences.i: and all that haunt the wide, clear lakes and all that haunt the thorny countryside, laid to rest in sleep beneath the silent night, [were easing their cares, their hearts forgetful of toil.]
sentences.n: 'quaeque… quaeque': the double '-que' ('both… and', 'those that… and those that'); 'quae' is feminine plural, 'those creatures', agreeing with 'positae'. 'lacus late liquidos' and 'rura… aspera dumis' ('rough with thickets', ablative) are the objects of 'tenent'. 'positae' ('laid down') agrees with the subject, and 'somno' is an ablative. Line 528 is printed in square brackets: Greenough marks it as spurious (not Virgil's). Without it 'positae' has no finite verb to go with; the bracketed line supplies 'lenibant', 'were soothing'. The bracketed words are kept here as Greenough prints them. 'oblita laborum' is a perfect participle with a genitive: 'forgetful of toils'.

sentences.t:
At non infelix animi Phoenissa, nec umquam
Solvitur in somnos, oculisve aut pectore noctem
accipit:
sentences.l:
But not the unhappy in spirit Phoenician woman, nor ever
is she loosed into sleep, or with eyes or with breast the night
receives:
sentences.i: But not so the Phoenician woman, unhappy in her heart: she is never released into sleep, nor takes the night in with eyes or breast;
sentences.n: 'At non' sets Dido against the sleeping world. 'infelix animi' is a genitive (or old locative) of respect, 'unhappy in mind', and 'Phoenissa' is a name for Dido, a Phoenician (Tyrian) woman. 'nec umquam' ('and never') is Greenough's 'nec'; the Latin Library prints 'neque'. 'Solvitur in somnos' is a passive with reflexive sense, 'is released into sleep'. 'oculisve aut pectore' offers two ablatives of means, 'with eyes or with breast', for how she takes in the night. The colon introduces an explanation.

sentences.t:
ingeminant curae, rursusque resurgens
saevit amor, magnoque irarum fluctuat aestu.
sentences.l:
cares redouble, and rising again
love rages, and with a great tide of angers it heaves.
sentences.i: Her cares redouble; love, surging up again, rages, and tosses on a great swell of anger.
sentences.n: 'ingeminant' is 'redouble', and 'resurgens' is a present participle ('rising again'), agreeing with 'amor'. 'saevit' ('rages') and 'fluctuat' ('heaves like a wave') both belong to 'amor'. 'irarum' is a plural of the abstract noun ('angers', poetic plural), and 'aestu' is an ablative of manner, 'with a tide'. Mercury will use almost these words of her at 564 ('varioque irarum fluctuat aestu'), so the god sees what the poet sees.

sentences.t: Sic adeo insistit, secumque ita corde volutat:
sentences.l: Thus indeed she persists, and with herself thus in her heart turns it over:
sentences.i: So she persists, and so she turns the matter over in her heart:
sentences.n: 'Sic adeo': 'adeo' is an intensifier, 'just so'. 'insistit' means 'persists, stands fast', and the verb of speaking is missing: 'secum… volutat' ('rolls it over with herself') leads into the speech without one. 'volutat' is a frequentative of 'volvo', for repeated rolling over in the mind. The colon opens her soliloquy.

sentences.t: “En, quid ago?
sentences.l: “See, what am I doing?
sentences.i: “Look at me: what am I doing?
sentences.n: The speech opens here and Greenough closes it at 552 (the closing mark falls at the end of that line). This line begins a new paragraph. Dido speaks to herself, in a string of questions in which the verbs are deliberative subjunctives ('what am I to do?'). 'En' is an interjection, 'Look!'; 'quid ago' ('what am I doing?') is in the indicative, and the questions that follow are the answer she gives herself.

sentences.t:
Rursusne procos inrisa priores
experiar, Nomadumque petam conubia supplex,
quos ego sim totiens iam dedignata maritos?
sentences.l:
Shall I again my former suitors, mocked,
make trial of, and of the Nomads seek the marriages, a suppliant,
whom I so often already have scorned as husbands?
sentences.i: Shall I, laughed at, turn again to try my former suitors, and as a suppliant seek a marriage among the Nomads, men whom I have so often scorned as husbands?
sentences.n: 'Rursusne… experiar… petam' are deliberative subjunctives ('shall I?'), with the enclitic '-ne' on 'rursus' marking the question. 'inrisa' is Greenough's spelling of 'irrisa', 'mocked' (by Aeneas, as she will say at 591); it agrees with the 'I' of 'experiar' (Dido), and 'priores procos' ('former suitors') is split by it. The Nomads are the Numidians, led by Iarbas, whom she had refused (196 and following). 'quos ego sim… dedignata maritos' is a relative clause with the subjunctive that gives a reason: 'since I have so often scorned them as husbands'. 'maritos' is predicative, 'as husbands'.

sentences.t:
Iliacas igitur classes atque ultima Teucrum
iussa sequar?
sentences.l:
The Ilian fleets, then, and the Teucrians' last
commands shall I follow?
sentences.i: Shall I, then, follow the fleet of Ilium and obey the Trojans' last commands?
sentences.n: 'Iliacas… classes' ('Trojan fleets'; the Latin Library has 'classis') and 'Teucrum' (old genitive plural for 'Teucrorum', as with 'Danaum' in earlier parts) name the Trojans: Ilium is Troy, and the Teucrians are Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer. 'ultima… iussa' ('final commands') may mean the last and lowest, to the end of their orders, in which case she asks whether she is to be their servant; 'sequar' is another deliberative subjunctive.

sentences.t:
Quiane auxilio iuvat ante levatos,
et bene apud memores veteris stat gratia facti?
sentences.l:
Is it because it pleases those before relieved by aid,
and well with the mindful stands gratitude for an old deed?
sentences.i: Is it because those whom my help once relieved are glad of it, and because gratitude for an old kindness stands firm among men who remember?
sentences.n: The irony is bitter: she asks whether she should follow them because they remember her kindness. 'Quiane' is 'quia' with '-ne': 'is it because?'. 'iuvat' is impersonal, 'it pleases', and 'levatos' agrees with an unexpressed 'eos', the Trojans, 'those relieved'; she had given them shelter and supplies when they were shipwrecked. The construction is loose ('iuvat' could also be taken as 'it helps'). 'apud memores' means 'among the mindful' (those who remember), and 'stat' is 'stands firm'. 'veteris… facti' is her own early kindness, 'old deed'.

sentences.t:
Quis me autem, fac velle, sinet, ratibusve superbis
invisam accipiet?
sentences.l:
Who, moreover, me — suppose I wish it — will allow, or on proud ships
hated will receive?
sentences.i: And who, granting that I wish it, will let me go, or take a woman they hate aboard their haughty ships?
sentences.n: 'fac velle' is 'suppose (that I) wish', with 'fac' the imperative of 'facio' used to mean 'suppose, grant' and an infinitive (its accusative 'me' is left out). 'me' is the object of 'sinet' ('will permit', with 'go' understood) and of 'accipiet'; 'ratibusve' is 'or on the ships', with enclitic '-ve'. 'invisam' ('hated') agrees with 'me'. 'superbis' echoes 'superbum' of her message (424): the Trojans are proud, in her eyes.

sentences.t:
Nescis heu, perdita, necdum
Laomedonteae sentis periuria gentis?
sentences.l:
Do you not know, alas, lost one, and not yet
the Laomedontean race's perjuries do you perceive?
sentences.i: Do you not know, alas, doomed woman, and do you not yet feel the perjuries of the race of Laomedon?
sentences.n: She addresses herself: 'perdita' ('lost, ruined') is a vocative; 'heu' is an exclamation of grief. 'Laomedonteae' is an adjective from Laomedon, the king of Troy who cheated Apollo and Neptune of their pay for building the city's walls (and Hercules, later); 'Laomedonteae periuria gentis' came to be a byword for Trojan bad faith. 'necdum' ('and not yet') goes with 'sentis'.

sentences.t:
Quid tum, sola fuga nautas comitabor ovantes,
an Tyriis omnique manu stipata meorum
inferar, et, quos Sidonia vix urbe revelli,
rursus agam pelago, et ventis dare vela iubebo?
sentences.l:
What then — alone in flight shall I accompany the exulting sailors,
or with the Tyrians and with all the band of my own, thronged,
shall I be borne in, and those whom from the Sidonian city I scarce tore away,
again shall I drive to the sea, and bid them give sails to the winds?
sentences.i: What then? Shall I go alone, in flight, with the exulting sailors, or be carried aboard with the Tyrians about me and all my own band, and drive once more out to sea the men I could scarcely tear from their Sidonian city, and bid them spread their sails to the winds?
sentences.n: 'Quid tum' means 'what then?', and the alternative question runs 'sola… an… stipata': 'sola fuga' is 'alone, in flight' (an ablative of manner); 'comitabor' is a deponent, 'shall I accompany'; 'ovantes' is 'exulting', the word used also in Aeneas's speech at 577 (the Latin Library has 'ovantis'). 'Tyriis omnique manu stipata meorum' is 'thronged by the Tyrians and by all the band of my own'. 'inferar' is the passive of 'infero' used reflexively, 'shall I be carried in' (onto the ships). 'Sidonia… urbe' is Tyre ('Sidonian' is used for 'Phoenician'). 'revelli' (perfect of 'revello') sits inside the relative clause; the main verbs 'agam' and 'iubebo' continue the series of questions in the future.

sentences.t: Quin morere, ut merita es, ferroque averte dolorem.
sentences.l: Nay rather die, as you have deserved, and with the sword turn aside your grief.
sentences.i: No — die, as you deserve, and drive your pain away with the sword.
sentences.n: 'Quin' with an imperative means 'why not rather…' or 'nay rather'. 'morere' is the imperative of the deponent 'morior'; 'ut merita es' is 'as you have deserved' (deponent 'mereor', perfect 'merita es'). 'ferro' is an ablative of means, 'with the sword', and 'averte' means 'turn aside'. She now says in so many words that she should die.

sentences.t:
Tu lacrimis evicta meis, tu prima furentem
his, germana, malis oneras atque obicis hosti.
sentences.l:
You, by my tears overcome, you first, me raging,
with these ills, sister, load and throw in the way of the enemy.
sentences.i: It was you, sister, you, won over by my tears, who first loaded me in my frenzy with these woes and threw me in the enemy's path.
sentences.n: 'Tu… tu' is anaphora, and the vocative 'germana' ('sister', Anna) is held back. 'evicta' agrees with 'tu' and means 'overcome', here 'won over'. 'prima' is a predicative adjective, 'first' (as in 'you were the first to'); 'furentem' agrees with an unexpressed 'me'. 'his… malis' is an ablative with 'oneras', 'load with'. 'obicis hosti' means 'you throw me in the path of (expose me to) the enemy'. The accusation is that Anna, at the beginning (31 and following), urged Dido to give in to her love.

sentences.t:
Non licuit thalami expertem sine crimine vitam
degere, more ferae, tales nec tangere curas!
sentences.l:
It was not granted, of the marriage-chamber unknowing, without reproach, a life
to pass, in the manner of a wild beast, and not to touch such cares!
sentences.i: I was not permitted to pass my life blameless, untouched by the marriage-chamber, like a wild creature, and never to meet cares such as these!
sentences.n: 'licuit' is the perfect of the impersonal 'licet', with the infinitives 'degere' and 'tangere' as its subjects. 'expertem' is an adjective with a genitive ('thalami expertem', 'without experience of the bridal chamber') and agrees with 'vitam': a life innocent of marriage. 'sine crimine' means 'without reproach'. 'more ferae' is 'in the manner of a wild animal', which lives without marriage. 'tales' is Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library has 'talis'. The sentence is an exclamation, not a question.

sentences.t: Non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo!”
sentences.l: Not kept is the faith promised to the ashes of Sychaeus!”
sentences.i: The faith I promised to the ashes of Sychaeus has not been kept!”
sentences.n: 'Non servata' has 'est' left out, and 'cineri… Sychaeo' ('to the ashes of Sychaeus') is the dative with 'promissa'. Sychaeus is Dido's first husband, murdered by her brother Pygmalion; she swore to keep faith with his memory (4.24–29). The closing quotation mark is Greenough's: the soliloquy ends here. This may be the grief under the others.

sentences.t: Tantos illa suo rumpebat pectore questus.
sentences.l: Such great laments she was breaking from her own breast.
sentences.i: Such were the laments she burst from her heart.
sentences.n: The poet's voice again after the speech: 'rumpebat' is an imperfect, 'was breaking forth', and 'questus' is the accusative plural of the fourth-declension noun 'questus', 'complaints, laments'. 'Tantos… questus' frames the line, with 'suo pectore' an ablative of separation.

sentences.t:
Aeneas celsa in puppi, iam certus eundi,
carpebat somnos, rebus iam rite paratis.
sentences.l:
Aeneas on the lofty stern, now sure of going,
was taking sleep, things now duly prepared.
sentences.i: Aeneas, high on the stern of his ship, already settled on departure, was taking his sleep, with everything duly made ready.
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough, and the scene changes to the Trojan ships. 'certus eundi' is an adjective with the genitive of the gerund of 'eo', 'sure of going'; 'rebus… paratis' is an ablative absolute, 'things having been prepared', and 'rite' means 'properly'. 'carpebat somnos' answers 'carpebant… soporem' at 522: while Dido cannot sleep, he can.

sentences.t:
Huic se forma dei voltu redeuntis eodem
obtulit in somnis, rursusque ita visa monere est—
sentences.l:
To him the form of a god, in the same face returning,
presented itself in dreams, and again thus seemed to warn —
sentences.i: To him the form of the god appeared in his sleep, with the face he had before, and again seemed to give him warning —
sentences.n: 'Huic se… obtulit' ('presented itself to him') takes the reflexive. 'dei' is Mercury, named in the next line; he had come to Aeneas before to order him to leave (4.265–276), which is why the face is 'eodem' ('the same') and the visit is 'rursus' ('again'). 'redeuntis' ('returning') is a present participle, agreeing with 'dei'. 'visa… est' (the passive of 'video', 'seem') is split by 'monere', and means 'seemed to warn'. 'voltu' is Greenough's spelling (the Latin Library prints 'uultu'). The dash breaks off the sentence to describe the god.

sentences.t:
omnia Mercurio similis, vocemque coloremque
et crinis flavos et membra decora iuventa:
sentences.l:
in all things like Mercury, both voice and colour
and yellow hair and limbs fair with youth:
sentences.i: in every respect like Mercury — the voice, the complexion, the yellow hair, the limbs lovely with youth:
sentences.n: 'omnia' is an accusative of respect, 'in all things', and 'Mercurio' is the dative with 'similis'. 'vocemque coloremque' and the following accusatives 'crinis' ('-is' for '-es', accusative plural), 'flavos' and 'membra' all depend in the same way ('similar as to voice, colour…'). 'decora' agrees with 'membra' ('fair, graceful'), and 'iuventa' is an ablative of respect, 'with youth'. The line is hypermetric: its last syllable, '-que', is elided into the 'et' that opens 559. The colon opens the god's speech.

sentences.t:
“Nate dea, potes hoc sub casu ducere somnos,
nec, quae te circum stent deinde pericula, cernis,
demens, nec Zephyros audis spirare secundos?
sentences.l:
“Goddess-born, can you under this chance draw out sleep,
nor, what perils may stand around you next, do you see,
madman, nor do you hear the Zephyrs breathing fair?
sentences.i: “Son of a goddess, can you go on sleeping in such a plight, and, madman, never see what perils will rise about you next, nor hear the fair west winds blowing?
sentences.n: Mercury's speech begins here and runs to 570. 'Nate dea' ('goddess-born', Venus's son) is how Mercury addresses Aeneas. 'hoc sub casu' means 'in this crisis', 'ducere somnos' means 'to draw out sleep'. 'quae… stent' is an indirect question with a subjunctive ('what perils may stand'); 'demens' is a vocative dropped into the middle of the clause; 'nec… nec' pairs the two negatives. The Zephyrs are the west winds, fair for the passage to Italy.

sentences.t:
Illa dolos dirumque nefas in pectore versat,
certa mori, varioque irarum fluctuat aestu.
sentences.l:
She treacheries and dread outrage in her breast turns over,
sure to die, and by a shifting tide of angers is tossed.
sentences.i: She is turning over schemes and a dreadful crime in her heart, resolved on death, and tossing on a shifting tide of rage.
sentences.n: 'dolos dirumque nefas' means 'treacheries and a dreadful wrong'; 'nefas' is a wrong that breaks divine law, and the god leaves it unnamed. 'versat' is 'turns over', and 'certa mori' is an adjective with an infinitive, 'sure to die' (compare 'certus eundi' at 554). 'varioque irarum fluctuat aestu' repeats 532 with 'vario' for 'magno'; the Latin Library prints a different second half, 'variosque… concitat aestus' ('stirs up shifting tides'), much the same picture.

sentences.t: Non fugis hinc praeceps, dum praecipitare potestas?
sentences.l: Do you not flee from here headlong, while to hasten is possible?
sentences.i: Will you not rush away from here, while rushing is still possible?
sentences.n: 'praeceps' is a predicative adjective, 'headlong', and 'praecipitare' makes a play on it: 'while it is possible to make haste'. 'dum' with the present indicative means 'while', and 'potestas' stands without 'est'. 'Non fugis' is a question that urges, 'will you not flee?'.

sentences.t:
Iam mare turbari trabibus, saevasque videbis
conlucere faces, iam fervere litora flammis,
si te his attigerit terris Aurora morantem.
sentences.l:
Soon the sea to be churned by timbers, and fierce you will see
torches to gleam, soon to seethe the shores with flames,
if you upon these lands Dawn shall have touched, lingering.
sentences.i: Soon you will see the sea churned by ships' timbers, savage torches blazing, the shores seething with flame, if Dawn's first light touches you still delaying in these lands.
sentences.n: 'turbari', 'conlucere' and 'fervere' are infinitives after 'videbis' ('you will see… the sea churned up'). 'saevasque… faces' is split, 'fierce torches'; 'trabibus' ('beams') stands for ships, and 'turbari trabibus' is 'to be thrown into turmoil by timbers' (oars, hulls). 'si… attigerit' is a future perfect: 'if Dawn shall have touched you'; 'morantem' agrees with 'te'. 'his… terris' is an ablative of place. The dawn comes at 584, but by then the fleet is gone.

sentences.t: Heia age, rumpe moras.
sentences.l: Come now, come, break off your delays.
sentences.i: Up, then — break off your delay!
sentences.n: 'Heia age' is an interjection of urging, 'come on, come!'; 'rumpe moras' is an idiom, 'break off delays'. It is the last and most urgent of the god's commands.

sentences.t:
Varium et mutabile semper
femina.
sentences.l:
Changeable and fickle always
a woman.”
sentences.i: Always a wavering, shifting creature is woman.”
sentences.n: 'Varium et mutabile' are neuter adjectives used as a predicate, 'a thing changeable and fickle', although the subject, 'femina', is feminine: the neuter treats woman as a type, not a person. Latin puts 'semper' ('always') before 'femina'. The line is a famous one; it is Mercury who speaks, not Virgil, and the reader may set it beside his 'certa mori' (564), 'sure to die'. The closing quotation mark is printed in Greenough after 'femina.' and before 'Sic', as here.

sentences.t: ”Sic fatus, nocti se immiscuit atrae.
sentences.l: Thus having spoken, with dark night he mingled himself.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and merged himself into the black night.
sentences.n: 'fatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'for', 'having spoken', the usual way to close a speech. 'nocti… atrae' is a dative with the compound verb 'immiscuit' ('mingled himself with'); 'ater' is the dull black of night and death. Mercury vanishes as a dream does.

sentences.t:
Tum vero Aeneas, subitis exterritus umbris,
corripit e somno corpus, sociosque fatigat:
sentences.l:
Then indeed Aeneas, by the sudden shadows terrified,
snatches from sleep his body, and his comrades rouses:
sentences.i: Then indeed Aeneas, terrified by the sudden shadows, tore himself from sleep and roused his comrades:
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'Tum vero' marks a turn, 'then indeed'. 'subitis exterritus umbris' means 'terrified by the sudden shades' (the dream-figure and the darkness it disappeared into), and 'umbris' is an ablative of cause. 'corripit e somno corpus' is 'snatches his body from sleep', and 'fatigat' means 'wears out' and so 'harries, rouses'. The colon introduces his short speech.

sentences.t: “Praecipites vigilate, viri, et considite transtris;
sentences.l: “Headlong, wake, men, and sit down at the benches;
sentences.i: “Wake in haste, men, and take your places at the rowing-benches;
sentences.n: Aeneas's speech opens here and Greenough closes it at 579. 'Praecipites' is a predicative adjective, 'headlong, in haste' (the Latin Library prints 'praecipitis', a different case-ending for the same sense); 'vigilate' is an imperative, 'be awake'; 'considite' means 'sit down' and 'transtris' is the rowers' benches, 'transtra'. The commands follow one another, as in Dido's reply later.

sentences.t: solvite vela citi.
sentences.l: loose the sails, quick.
sentences.i: loose the sails, and quickly.
sentences.n: 'citi' is a nominative plural of the adjective 'citus', 'quick', agreeing with the understood 'you' (Latin uses an adjective where English has an adverb). 'solvite vela' means 'loose the sails'. The unit is short because the sentence breaks at the full stop in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
Deus aethere missus ab alto
festinare fugam tortosque incidere funes
ecce iterum stimulat.
sentences.l:
A god, from lofty ether sent,
to hasten flight and the twisted ropes to cut,
lo, again urges.
sentences.i: Look, a god sent from the heights of the sky is once more goading us to speed our flight and sever the twisted hawsers.
sentences.n: 'Deus… missus' is the subject, 'a god sent', and the verb 'stimulat' ('goads') waits until the end of the sentence; 'ecce iterum' says it is the second time he comes. 'festinare' and 'incidere' are infinitives depending on 'stimulat', 'goads to hurry… to cut'. 'festinare fugam' makes 'fugam' the object ('hurry the flight'). 'tortos… funes' is the twisted ropes (cables); 'funes' is Greenough's, the Latin Library has 'funis'. 'stimulat' (the Latin Library prints 'instimulat') is a verb of urging. The god is Mercury, but Aeneas does not know who it was ('quisquis es', 577).

sentences.t:
Sequimur te, sancte deorum,
quisquis es, imperioque iterum paremus ovantes.
sentences.l:
We follow you, holy of gods,
whoever you are, and to your command again we obey, rejoicing.
sentences.i: We follow you, holy one among the gods, whoever you are, and once more we obey your bidding with joy.
sentences.n: 'sancte deorum' is a vocative with a partitive genitive plural, 'holy one among the gods'. 'quisquis es' ('whoever you are') is the formula used when the speaker does not know the name or title of the god. 'imperio… paremus' takes the dative with 'pareo' ('obey'), and 'iterum' means 'once more' (he obeyed Mercury the first time). 'ovantes' ('exulting') is in the nominative plural, agreeing with the subject 'we'; it is the same word Dido used of these sailors (543).

sentences.t:
Adsis o placidusque iuves, et sidera caelo
dextra feras.
sentences.l:
Be present, O, and gently help, and stars in the sky
auspicious bring.”
sentences.i: Be near us and graciously help us, and bring favouring stars in the sky.”
sentences.n: 'Adsis', 'iuves' and 'feras' are present subjunctives that express a wish ('may you be present…'). 'placidus' is a predicative adjective, 'graciously'. 'dextra' is a neuter plural, 'auspicious' ('right-hand', hence 'favourable'), and 'sidera caelo dextra feras' is 'may you bring favourable stars in the sky'. The closing quotation mark falls after the period, as in the printed text.

sentences.t:
”Dixit, vaginaque eripit ensem
fulmineum, strictoque ferit retinacula ferro.
sentences.l:
He said, and from the sheath snatches the sword
lightning-like, and with the drawn steel strikes the cables.
sentences.i: He spoke, and snatched his lightning-bright sword from its sheath and struck at the cables with the drawn blade.
sentences.n: 'Dixit' is a perfect, closing the speech. 'vagina' is an ablative of separation without a preposition, 'from the sheath'; 'fulmineum' ('lightning-like') agrees with 'ensem' and is split from it by the line break. 'stricto… ferro' is an ablative of means, 'with the drawn iron'; 'ferro' is a word for steel by its material. 'retinacula' are the mooring cables that hold the ship to the shore. Aeneas does not wait to untie them.

sentences.t: Idem omnes simul ardor habet, rapiuntque ruuntque;
sentences.l: The same ardour holds all at once, and they snatch and rush;
sentences.i: The same eagerness grips them all at once; they seize their tasks and hurry on;
sentences.n: 'Idem omnes simul ardor habet' has 'idem… ardor' ('the same ardour') as its subject, with 'omnes simul' ('all at once') set between the two words. 'omnes' is Greenough's, the Latin Library has 'omnis'. 'rapiunt' has no object ('they seize', they take up the work) and 'ruunt' means 'rush'; the double '-que… -que' ('both… and') gives a breathless pace, and the line is full of short syllables.

sentences.t: litora deseruere; latet sub classibus aequor;
sentences.l: The shores they have left; hidden is beneath the fleets the sea;
sentences.i: They have left the shores behind, and the sea is hidden beneath the fleet;
sentences.n: 'deseruere' is 'deseruerunt', the '-ere' ending for '-erunt' (you will see it constantly). 'classibus' is a plural for 'the fleet' (poetic plural), and 'latet sub classibus aequor' means that the sea is covered by the ships. The two clauses in a single line are separated by a semicolon.

sentences.t: adnixi torquent spumas et caerula verrunt.
sentences.l: Straining, they twist the foam and sweep the blue.
sentences.i: Straining at the oars, they whirl up the foam and sweep the dark water.
sentences.n: 'adnixi' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'adnitor' ('lean, strain'), 'having leaned (on the oars)'. 'torquent spumas' is 'twist the foam' and 'caerula' ('the blue (parts)') is a neuter plural used as a noun, 'verrunt' meaning 'sweep', the way the oars brush the sea. The line is repeated word for word at 3.208.

sentences.t:
Et iam prima novo spargebat lumine terras
Tithoni croceum linquens Aurora cubile.
sentences.l:
And now the early with new light was scattering the lands
Tithonus's saffron bed leaving, Dawn.
sentences.i: And now, quitting Tithonus' saffron couch, early Dawn was strewing fresh light across the lands.
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'prima… Aurora' is split across the two lines ('early Dawn'); 'novo lumine' is an ablative of means, and 'spargebat' is imperfect, 'was scattering'. 'Tithoni' is the husband of Dawn: a Trojan prince whom she loved, and for whom she obtained immortality but not ageless youth. 'croceum' means 'saffron-coloured', the colour of dawn. The pair of lines is used again at 9.459–460. 'iam' picks up Mercury's warning ('si te… Aurora morantem', 568): morning has come and the Trojans are gone.

sentences.t:
Regina e speculis ut primum albescere lucem
vidit, et aequatis classem procedere velis,
litoraque et vacuos sensit sine remige portus,
sentences.l:
The queen from the watch-towers, when first to whiten the light
she saw, and with sails evened the fleet to advance,
and the shores and the empty harbours perceived without oarsman,
sentences.i: As soon as the queen saw from her watch-towers the daylight whiten and the fleet moving out with sails trimmed evenly, and knew the shores and harbours to be empty, without a single oarsman,
sentences.n: 'ut primum' means 'as soon as' and takes the perfect 'vidit' and 'sensit' ('saw… perceived'). 'e speculis' means 'from the watch-towers' (plural), and 'albescere' and 'procedere' are infinitives after 'vidit'. 'aequatis… velis' is an ablative absolute: sails 'made equal', i.e. trimmed to catch the wind equally. 'litora… et vacuos… portus' are the objects of 'sensit', and 'sine remige' is 'without a rower' (singular for 'oarsmen'). The main verb, 'ait', does not come until 591. The Latin Library prints 'primam' for Greenough's 'primum', which gives much the same picture ('the first light').

sentences.t:
terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum,
flaventesque abscissa comas,
sentences.l:
three times and four with her hand her breast, comely, having struck,
and her yellow locks having torn off,
sentences.i: having struck her fair breast with her hand three times and four, and torn her golden hair,
sentences.n: 'percussa' and 'abscissa' are perfect passive participles with the accusatives of respect 'pectus' and 'comas' ('having struck herself as to the breast', 'having torn herself as to the hair'): the same use as at 509 and 518. 'terque quaterque' is a set formula, 'three times and four', for 'over and over' (compare I.94). 'decorum' is 'comely' and agrees with 'pectus'; 'flaventes' ('golden-yellow', Greenough's; the Latin Library 'flauentisque') agrees with 'comas'. Beating the breast and tearing the hair are the gestures of grief.

sentences.t:
“Pro Iuppiter, ibit
“hic ait et nostris inluserit advena regnis?
sentences.l:
“O Jupiter, he will go
this man, she says, and at our realms a stranger will have mocked?
sentences.i: “Great Jupiter! Shall he go, this man, she says, and a stranger have made sport of my kingdom?
sentences.n: Dido's speech opens here at 590 ('Pro Iuppiter') and runs on to 606 and beyond the end of this part, without a closing mark in Greenough; Greenough prints a second opening mark before 'hic' in 591, and the archive prints the marks as they stand. 'ibit hic' is 'he will go, this man' (Aeneas), with the poet's 'ait' ('she says') dropped into the middle of her words. 'Pro' is an interjection, 'O!' with the vocative. 'ibit' is a future used as an indignant question, 'shall he go?'; 'inluserit' is a future perfect, 'will have mocked', and takes the dative 'regnis' ('at my realms'); 'advena' ('stranger, newcomer') is her bitter name for Aeneas.

sentences.t:
Non arma expedient, totaque ex urbe sequentur,
deripientque rates alii navalibus?
sentences.l:
Will they not make arms ready, and from the whole city follow,
and snatch down the ships, others, from the docks?
sentences.i: Will they not get out their arms and pour from the whole city in pursuit, while others drag the ships down from the dockyards?
sentences.n: 'Non… expedient… sequentur… deripient' is a series of questions in the future with 'non', which have the force of commands: 'will they not…?', i.e. 'let them!'. 'expedio' means 'get ready'; 'alii' ('others') is the subject of 'deripient' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library has 'diripient'), 'snatch down'. 'navalibus' is an ablative of separation, 'from the dockyards' ('navalia', the slips where ships are kept).

sentences.t:
Ite,
ferte citi flammas, date vela, impellite remos!—
sentences.l:
Go,
bring quick flames, give sails, drive on oars! —
sentences.i: Go, bring fire quickly, spread the sails, drive on the oars! —
sentences.n: 'Ite' is the imperative of 'eo'. The commands come without a conjunction (asyndeton), as in an order shouted in a crisis: 'ferte', 'date', 'impellite'. 'citi' is 'quick' (an adjective for an adverb, as at 574). Greenough's 'vela' stands against the Latin Library's 'tela' (spears); the Latin Library's reading would make the order 'give spears' where Greenough has 'give sails'. The dash breaks off her shouting: she checks herself.

sentences.t: Quid loquor, aut ubi sum? Quae mentem insania mutat?
sentences.l: What am I saying, or where am I? What madness changes my mind?
sentences.i: What am I saying? Where am I? What madness is altering my mind?
sentences.n: The sudden break in her mood. 'aut' ('or') joins two linked questions: 'what am I saying, or (rather) where am I?'. 'mentem mutat' means 'changes (my) mind'. Dido's own self-reproach is as much a part of her as her anger.

sentences.t: Infelix Dido, nunc te facta impia tangunt.
sentences.l: Unhappy Dido, now you impious deeds touch.
sentences.i: Unhappy Dido, only now do impious deeds touch you.
sentences.n: 'Infelix' is the same adjective as at 529. 'facta impia' ('impious deeds') can be read either as her own broken faith to Sychaeus, or as Aeneas's treachery: the next line, 'Tum decuit, cum sceptra dabas', suggests the point is her having given him the sceptre, and either reading works. 'tangunt' means 'touch, affect'.

sentences.t:
Tum decuit, cum sceptra dabas.—En dextra fidesque,
quem secum patrios aiunt portare Penates,
quem subiisse umeris confectum aetate parentem!
sentences.l:
Then it was fitting, when you were giving the sceptres. — Behold the right hand and the faith,
of him whom with himself, they say, his fathers' Penates he carries,
whom to have borne up on his shoulders, spent with age, his father!
sentences.i: That was the time to feel it, when you were giving him the sceptre. — Behold the right hand, behold the faith of him who, they say, carries his ancestral gods about with him, who took his aged father upon his shoulders!
sentences.n: 'decuit' is an impersonal perfect, 'it was fitting', with the infinitive understood ('to be touched'); 'tum' is 'then', and 'cum… dabas' is 'when you were giving' (the imperfect indicative with 'cum' of a time). 'sceptra' is a poetic plural. Her point is that she gave him a share in her rule and her city: Mercury found him founding its citadels and building new houses (4.260). The dash marks another break in her thought. 'En dextra fidesque' means 'Behold the right hand and the pledged faith (of)…', with the relative 'quem' standing as though 'eius' had been written first: the syntax is loose, as in an outburst. 'quem… aiunt portare… quem subiisse… parentem' puts both 'portare' and 'subiisse' (from 'subeo') in the accusative and infinitive after 'aiunt' ('they say'), with 'quem' as their accusative subject. 'aiunt' ('they say') may be bitter: she doubts the legend of his piety. 'patrios… Penates' are the household gods of Troy, which Aeneas carried from the burning city together with his father Anchises on his back (Book 2). 'confectum aetate' ('worn out by age') agrees with 'parentem'. Greenough's 'Penates' stands against the Latin Library's 'penatis' (accusative plural in '-is').

sentences.t:
Non potui abreptum divellere corpus, et undis
spargere?
sentences.l:
Could I not, the body snatched away, tear it apart, and over the waves
scatter it?
sentences.i: Could I not have carried him off, torn the body apart and scattered it over the waves?
sentences.n: 'Non potui' means 'was I not able?', 'could I not have?'; 'abreptum… corpus' has 'abreptum' as a participle agreeing with 'corpus' ('the body snatched away'), so 'seize and tear apart'. 'divellere' and 'spargere' are the infinitives after 'potui'. The picture recalls Medea, who in the myth tore her brother Absyrtus to pieces and scattered his limbs on the sea to delay her father's pursuit.

sentences.t:
Non socios, non ipsum absumere ferro
Ascanium, patriisque epulandum ponere mensis?—
sentences.l:
Not his comrades, not himself to make away with by the sword,
Ascanius, and to be feasted on to set on his father's tables? —
sentences.i: Could I not have put his comrades and Ascanius himself to the sword, and set the boy on his father's table to be feasted on? —
sentences.n: 'Non socios, non ipsum… Ascanium' continues the 'non potui' of the last question, which governs 'absumere' and 'ponere'. 'ipsum' and 'Ascanium' are split. 'epulandum' is a gerundive agreeing with 'Ascanium': 'to be feasted on'. 'patriis… mensis' means 'on his father's table(s)': the picture recalls the banquets of Atreus and Thyestes or of Tereus, where fathers ate their own children. The dash breaks the thought off: she cannot sustain the horror of her own fantasy.

sentences.t: Verum anceps pugnae fuerat fortuna:—fuisset.
sentences.l: But doubtful of the fight had been the fortune: — let it have been so.
sentences.i: But the fortune of the fight had been in doubt. — Granted: let it have been so.
sentences.n: 'anceps' ('two-headed, doubtful') agrees with 'fortuna'; 'fuerat' is a pluperfect, 'had been', set back to the time she is picturing. 'fuisset' is a pluperfect subjunctive standing alone: 'let it have been (so)', granted. She answers her own objection and puts it aside in the next question. The dash after the colon is Greenough's own.

sentences.t: Quem metui moritura?
sentences.l: Whom did I fear, about to die?
sentences.i: Whom did I fear, I who was about to die?
sentences.n: 'metui' is the perfect of 'metuo', 'did I fear?', and 'moritura' is a future participle ('about to die'), agreeing with the subject: she means that someone sure to die has nothing to fear. It echoes 'moritura' at 519 and 415.

sentences.t:
Faces in castra tulissem,
implessemque foros flammis, natumque patremque
cum genere extinxem, memet super ipsa dedissem.
sentences.l:
Torches into the camp I might have carried,
and filled the decks with flames, and the son and the father
with the race might have destroyed, myself on top, myself, might have given.
sentences.i: I would have carried torches into their camp, filled their decks with flame, wiped out son and father together with their race, and flung myself, myself, on top of them all.
sentences.n: 'tulissem', 'implessem' (for 'implevissem'), 'extinxem' (for 'extinxissem') and 'dedissem' are pluperfect subjunctives in a main clause, 'I would have', for what she failed to do; the shortened forms ('implessem', 'extinxem') come from dropping '-vi-' and '-is-', a regular contraction. 'foros' (accusative plural of 'forus') are the gangways or decks of a ship. 'natumque patremque cum genere' is 'son and father, together with their race'; Greenough's 'extinxem' stands for the Latin Library's 'exstinxem'. 'memet… ipsa' ('myself, I myself') doubles the emphasis, and 'super' ('on top of them') is an adverb; 'dedissem' with the reflexive means 'given myself (to death)', which says outright what she now wishes she had done. The speech goes on past the end of this part.
